children: By Staff Writer

The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) has eased interest rate from 26.5 percent to 23 percent in September, 2026, eliciting optimism from economists and capital markets experts on the positive outlook on economic growth.

Speaking at the 307th meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) in Abuja, Governor of CBN, Mr Olayemi Cardoso, said the committee examined recent trends in the global and domestic economic environment.
Before arriving at the new interest rate, Cardoso said, the committee considered emerging risks to the outlook and evaluated their potential implications for monetary policy.
“Eleven members of the committee were in attendance. The committee decided as follows: One, reset the monetary policy rate at 23 percent.

“Two, recalibrate the standing facilities corridor to plus 50 to minus 300 basis points around the MPC. Three, retain the cash reserve requirement for deposit money banks at 45 percent, merchant banks at 16 percent, and non-TSA public sector deposits at 75 percent. The policy corridor as an important operational realignment aimed at strengthening monetary policy transmission and reinforcing the primacy of the Monetary Policy Committee.”

The MPC also emphasised that the recalibration of the corridor does not constitute a change in the current monetary policy stance, but rather an operational reset to enhance the effectiveness of monetary policy and support the transition to an inflation-targeting regime.
According to MPC, “Members are of the view that the current macroeconomic environment remains supportive of such a recalibration without undermining the disinflation process.

“Considerations in arriving at this decision, the Committee noted that the observed divergence between the MPR and the prevailing market rates had weakened the effectiveness of monetary policy transmission.”

Cardoso said members of the MPC noted that the bank’s ongoing repair of the monetary policy implementation framework, including the adoption of NOFR as a transaction-based operational benchmark, has improved the transparency of money market operations.

“The Committee, therefore, considered a reset of the MPR and recalibration of the corridor appropriate to better align the monetary policy implementation framework with market realities. This would strengthen policy transmission and restore the MPR as the principal signal of monetary policy,” he stated.
Economists, capital market experts laud CBN

Meanwhile, MPC has been commended for cutting the Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) from 26.5 percent to 23 percent, with economists describing the 350-basis-point reduction as a balanced decision that could strengthen banking system resilience and support economic growth.

The economists commenting on the Capital Markets Academics Association of Nigeria platform said the decision effectively reduced the price of money and, alongside the recalibration of the Standing Facilities Corridor to +50/-300 basis points, could discourage banks from parking excess liquidity with the apex bank and encourage lending to productive sectors.
However, they cautioned that the impact of the rate cut would depend largely on how quickly monetary policy is transmitted to lending rates and the real economy.

Banker, lawyer and economist, Dr Suleyman A. Ndanusa, said the cut could reduce borrowing costs, ease government debt-service pressures and provide businesses and households with greater financial breathing space.
He described the 350-basis-point reduction as a “decisive policy reset” and a signal that the CBN was gradually shifting from emergency stabilisation towards supporting productive economic activity.
According to him, the recalibrated corridor means banks borrowing from the CBN will pay about 23.5 percent, while banks placing surplus funds with the apex bank will earn about 20 percent.
He said the narrower corridor should encourage banks to deploy liquidity into lending and interbank transactions rather than comfortably warehouse surplus funds with the CBN.

“The CBN has reduced the price of money but retained the formidable CRR barriers: 45 percent for deposit money banks, 16 percent for merchant banks and 75 percent on non-TSA public sector deposits,” Ndanusa said.
“In simple terms, the Bank has loosened the interest rate brake while keeping a firm grip on the liquidity handbrake. Therefore, cheaper credit to businesses may not arrive automatically or quickly.”
He said banks still faced high operating costs, credit risks and competition from government securities, which could remain attractive relative to lending to businesses.
Ndanusa said the real test of the MPC decision would be whether lending rates decline, credit reaches agriculture and manufacturing, and borrowing costs for small businesses fall.
He, however, urged the MPC to provide a clear analytical explanation for the size and timing of the rate cut, particularly regarding inflation, capital flows and exchange-rate risks.

Former Director, Bank Examination Department, Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC), Mike Onadele, also described the decision as “well judged and timely” from a prudential and financial system stability perspective.
Onadele said the rate cut was particularly significant following the completion of the banking sector recapitalisation, which had strengthened banks’ capital buffers.

He said retaining the Cash Reserve Requirement (CRR) at 45 percent for deposit money banks demonstrated the CBN’s continued focus on liquidity management and systemic resilience, while the lower MPR should moderate funding costs and improve balance-sheet efficiency.
He said stronger capital positions would provide banks with greater headroom to maintain high-quality liquid assets while expanding selective and appropriately priced lending to the real sector.
“The corridor adjustment further reinforces the MPR as the credible anchor for rate formation and strengthens monetary policy transmission,” he said.
He added that positioning the adjustment as an operational reset towards an inflation-targeting framework could improve policy clarity and credibility.

Meanwhile, researcher at Covenant University, Dr Ayinde O. Ayinde, said the rate cut could mark the beginning of a broader economic policy coordination framework, particularly against the backdrop of the recent fiscal and monetary policy coordination memorandum between the CBN and the Federal Ministry of Finance.
Ayinde said the significance of the policy would ultimately be measured by its impact on the cost of credit, household purchasing power, employment and business activity.

He noted that lower MPR could potentially reduce financing costs for mortgages, agriculture, enterprise loans, education, transportation and consumer expenditure, but stressed that transmission would not be automatic.
He said commercial banks would continue to price loans based on funding costs, liquidity, credit risks, capital requirements, collateral constraints and other risk premiums.

Ayinde said MSMEs would be critical to the transmission of cheaper money into the real economy, noting that lower effective borrowing costs could improve working capital, machinery acquisition, technological upgrades and business expansion.
He also warned that monetary easing could have distributional effects, with borrowers benefiting from lower financing costs while savers and fixed-income investors could face lower nominal returns.

According to him, the foreign exchange channel also requires careful monitoring because lower domestic interest rates could affect portfolio preferences, capital flows, demand for naira assets and exchange-rate expectations.

He urged the CBN, fiscal authorities and banks to monitor credit repricing, private-sector credit, sectoral lending, inflation expectations, exchange rates, government borrowing and household welfare.
The ultimate objective, he said, should be to convert cheaper money into productive capital, productive capital into employment and employment into stronger household incomes and purchasing power.

title: ZAWYA: The Central Bank of Nigeria eases interest rate to 23%
